newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Novice players lead Brazil stock retreat.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Novice players lead Brazil stock retreat.

text.p: Nervous, small-time investors who pushed Brazil's stock market to record highs this year are leading this week's panicked retreat, unable to bear the risk familiar to more seasoned players, analysts said.

"These newcomers don't have the experience or expertise to stick it out with a volatile asset like stocks. They are getting out at the first sign of trouble," said Craig Barley, international manager at Rio de Janeiro's Banco Omega.

Doctors, lawyers, teachers and other middle-class investors who traditionally put their savings in government bonds have over the past year shifted into more risky equity funds, some of which were offering annualized returns of over 100 percent.
The funds have grown more than 250 percent over the past 12 months and led the 90 percent gain in Brazil's stock market from January through mid-July.

Analysts said the nerves of these mom-and-pop investors got their first test early this week when rumors that currency turmoil in Asia could spread to Brazil caused Latin American markets to plunge on Tuesday in what has been called the "samba effect."

Despite assurances from the Brazilian government that there would be no devaluation and statements by economists who said fundamentals did not merit immediate concern, many investors decided to retreat.
"The local individual investors who have joined the market recently are definitely moving out," Barley said.
Since last Friday, Brazil's Bovespa stock index has plunged about 20 percent.
Selling on Tuesday and Thursday, according to traders and analysts, was driven by profit-taking and fund managers acting on client orders to get out of the market.
But Friday's sell-off was seen as a pre-emptive move on the part of fund managers who expect more investors to pull out of equity funds and return to fixed-income instruments.
While fund managers reported no exodus by individual investors on Friday, market players said funds were selling to raise cash for anticipated withdrawals next week.
"The big guys are just watching and we haven't seen any significant pullout by foreigners. This is a lot of mutual fund selling to raise cash for redemptions," said a trader at a Sao Paulo brokerage.
Market players said it was impossible to say when or if individuals would return to the market.
"It is difficult to say. Two days ago, I thought we were at the bottom of the trough, but that wasn't the case," said one analyst who asked not to be named.

Brazil's chaotic economic past discouraged many small-time investors from gambling in the stock market. Rather, they put their money into government fixed-income securities, which offered high yields and less risk.
Falling interest rates over the past 18 months, however, have made fixed-income yields less attractive and have encouraged a migration into equity funds.
